title: Test the knee jerk: swing a reflex hammer so it taps the tendon just below the kneecap briskly and lifts straight off
instruction: Test the knee-jerk reflex on the leg trainer: take the reflex hammer from its cup, tap the tendon just below the kneecap so the leg kicks, then stand the hammer back in its cup.
context: Having a doctor tap just below your kneecap with a rubber hammer, and watching your lower leg kick, is one of the most familiar moments of a check-up; physicians, nurse practitioners, physical therapists and nurses doing neurological checks use it to test the L2-L4 nerve roots. Clinical guides: hold the Taylor hammer at the end of its handle and swing it in an arc onto the tendon (maker's directions), "in a quick striking motion by the wrist", with "the broad end" on the patellar tendon between the kneecap and the tibial tubercle, knee partly flexed and supported. The reflex needs a brisk tap: in a 100-person study the knee's kick grew with the hammer's speed and was near zero for slow taps. So the robot must swing the head at about 1 m/s or more, land it within a band about 30 mm tall below the kneecap, not on the kneecap or the bone below, and let it come straight off rather than push.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the bench top. Leg trainer: a life-size adult right-leg trainer cut at mid-thigh, lying on its back on the bench with its foot away to the robot's front right (the leg's line points 60 degrees right of straight ahead). Its thigh stub is clamped to the bench and rests on an 80 mm foam roll (250 mm long, fixed) 90 mm above the knee; the knee's hinge is at (0.338, -0.062), 150 mm up; the knee is bent about 18 degrees (the thigh rises 8 degrees toward the knee, the shin falls 10 degrees to the heel) and the heel rests on the bench. The lower leg and foot (2 kg) swing freely on the knee's hinge, lightly damped, and lie on the heel under their own weight. Kneecap: 50 mm across, its front 62 mm above the knee's axis. Patellar tendon: a strip 28 mm wide running 45 mm down the shin from the kneecap's lower pole (12 mm below the knee's axis) to the tibial tubercle, a bump 6 mm proud of it. The strike band is the middle of the tendon: 17 to 47 mm below the knee's axis along the shin and within 15 mm of the tendon's midline; its centre is at (0.358, -0.096), 189 mm up. Reflex hammer: an ADC Taylor percussion hammer, 190 mm long and about 70 g: a flat chrome handle 12 mm wide and 3 mm thick, and a triangular red rubber head 50 mm long, 28 mm tall and 13 mm thick, its broad striking end on one side of the handle and its apex on the other. It stands head-down in a rigid desk cup (80 mm inside, 60 mm tall, fixed to the bench) centred at (0.215, -0.400), the handle's end up at 194 mm, the head's broad end toward the robot. Both arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: The knee jerk follows the trainer's reflex rule, as on a patient: a tap counts when the hammer is held in a gripper, its head (not the handle) touches the leg first with the broad face's centre over the strike band, it lands at 0.6 m/s or more into the skin, and it lifts off (5 mm clear) within 0.25 s. The lower leg then kicks (60 ms after landing, or at lift-off if later) by 10 degrees x (landing speed - 0.6) / 0.9, at most 10 degrees. A clear knee jerk is a kick of at least 5 degrees (the foot rises about 40 mm; a landing of about 1.05 m/s or more). Full score 1.0, ending the run: a clear knee jerk, and then the hammer stood back in its cup (its head inside the cup, below the rim) or laid on the bench (lowest point within 5 mm of the bench top), let go (no gripper within 30 mm of it) and still for 1 s. 0.75: a clear knee jerk, the hammer not yet put down and let go. 0.5: only a weak jerk (at least 1 degree; a landing of about 0.7 to 1.05 m/s). 0.25: the head landed on the band, held, but no jerk fired (too slow, or it stayed pressed on the tendon). 0 otherwise, including taps on the kneecap, the tubercle, the shin or the thigh, taps with the handle, and moving the leg by hand. 0 for the rest of the run if the hammer falls off the bench (lowest point 20 mm below the bench top).
run_limit: 1,200 steps (60 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo takes about 21 s
reset_notes: Let the lower leg settle onto its heel (it rests there by itself); stand the hammer head-down in its cup, handle end up, the head's broad end toward the robot.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. No muscle or nerve is simulated: the knee jerk is a rule in the task's code (a timed knee-extension speed fired by a brisk tap on the tendon band), its speed thresholds set from Tham et al. 2013. The leg, skin and rubber head are rigid primitives; the thigh, roll and cup are fixed. Estimates: the hammer's mass and sizes, the trainer's sizes, lower-leg mass and knee damping, and the band's size.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right arm reached toward the knee and the cup but never took the hammer, which stood in its cup to the end); demo: 1.0 (success at step 436)
